opus-5.5.text:
I think what makes audio exciting right now is that it feels a bit like where text was a few years ago. With text, a lot of the big questions have been explored quite heavily: scaling, data mixtures, post-training, reasoning. They're still important, but the low-hanging fruit is mostly gone. With audio there's still a lot of open territory, and you can have real impact with relatively simple ideas.

It's also a harder and richer signal than text. When you write something down you lose a huge amount of information: the tone, the emotion, the hesitations, who is speaking, the background noise, the timing. A good audio model has to deal with all of that at once. So you have interesting modeling questions. How do you tokenize audio well? How do you balance semantic content with acoustic detail? How do you deal with much longer sequences, since one second of audio carries far more tokens than a sentence of text? Those questions don't really come up in the same way for pure language models.

Then there's the product side, which I find very motivating. Voice is the most natural interface people have. If you want assistants that feel natural to talk to, with low latency, that can be interrupted and understand nuance in how you say something and not just what you say, then you need models that are native in audio, not a pipeline of speech-to-text, then an LLM, then text-to-speech. Every step in that pipeline loses information and adds latency. Getting rid of it end to end is a hard research problem, but when it works the difference is very obvious to users.

And finally, I think audio is a good test of whether our techniques generalize. A lot of what we learned from text, like next-token prediction, scaling, and instruction tuning, does transfer, but not perfectly. Seeing where it breaks teaches you something about the methods themselves. So for me it's both a practical area with real applications and a good place to learn things that feed back into language modeling more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response describes open research questions and several modeling challenges, but does not identify the variety of possible approaches to building audio models as a reason for his interest.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what draws me to audio is that it's a space where there's still a lot of low-hanging fruit. Text language models have been studied so intensely by so many people for so long that making a real step forward is hard. Every obvious idea has been tried. Audio is much less mature, so when you sit down and try something, there's a genuine chance it works and nobody has done it before. That feeling is quite rare now in text.

The second thing is that audio is a very natural modality for interacting with a model. When you talk to someone, you don't wait for them to finish, you interrupt, you overlap, you react to tone. Most "voice assistants" are really a pipeline: speech-to-text, then a text model, then text-to-speech. You lose latency, you lose emotion, you lose everything that isn't the words themselves. Building a model that actually operates in the audio domain end to end, that listens and speaks at the same time, in real time, is a really interesting research problem. The latency constraint alone changes how you think about the architecture.

And then there's the data question, which I find fascinating. In text, the way to get knowledge into a model is well understood: scrape a lot of it, pretrain, instruction-tune. For audio there's much less transcribed, high-quality conversational data, so you have to be clever. You have to think about synthetic data, about how to transfer knowledge from a text model into an audio one without losing what makes speech speech. That mix of modeling, systems constraints, and data engineering, where none of it is solved yet, is what makes it fun for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes audio as an immature area with room to try new ideas, then names several approaches—end-to-end audio modeling, synthetic data, and transferring knowledge from text models—as reasons the research is interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think audio is especially interesting because language is only part of the information in the signal. In text, you have the words. In speech, you also have intonation, emotion, pauses, and timing. You can say exactly the same sentence and mean something very different depending on how you say it.

That makes it an interesting modeling problem. How do you represent all that information, and how do you build a model that can respond naturally? A conversation is not just one person finishing a paragraph and then the other person starting. People interrupt, they hesitate, they give little signals that they’re listening. So there’s a lot to explore beyond getting the words right.

r001.rationale: The response discusses audio’s nonverbal information and conversational behavior as areas to explore, but does not identify the variety of approaches to building audio models as a reason for the interest.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find especially interesting about audio is that it forces you to think beyond text. When we speak, the words are only part of the information. There’s intonation, emotion, rhythm, pauses—all these things that disappear when you turn a conversation into a transcript.

And technically, it’s a very different problem. Audio is continuous, the sequences are much longer, and in a real conversation you have to respond with very low latency. You have to know when someone has finished speaking, when to wait, how to handle an interruption. So it’s not just about generating a good answer; it’s about participating in an interaction.

I think that combination is exciting: there are fundamental modeling questions, but the improvements are also immediately tangible. You can hear when an interaction starts to feel more natural.

r001.rationale: The response describes audio’s non-text information, technical challenges, and interactive qualities, but does not identify variety in approaches to building audio models as a reason for the interest.
